proposals.reason: The Japanese kobujime cure: raw fish is pressed between sheets of kelp, which draw out moisture, firm the flesh and season it with the kelp's glutamate. It appears on omakase and New American crudo menus. It is a specialist word that guests confuse with salt-curing (Cured) and with the deck's Koji-Aged, which uses mold enzymes, not seaweed. A senior server must keep those apart. No card, alias or Lexicon candidate covers kombu or kobujime. It belongs here beside Cured and Koji-Aged, as a curing verb.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does kombu-cured do to the fish? Is it cooked, and is it the same as koji?
proposals.menuLine: Kombu-Cured Fluke, Yuzu Kosho, Shiso, Puffed Rice

proposals.reason: The Japanese word for flame-seared. A blowtorch or binchotan touches only the surface of raw fish or wagyu, so the fat softens and the inside stays raw. It is printed on omakase and high-end sushi menus in America, and guests who know sushi test servers on it. Setting it apart from Seared (a hard crust in a hot pan) and from Tataki (seared all round, then sliced, taught in Preparations) takes a sentence, which is exactly the near-neighbor contrast this section teaches. The deck has neither the word nor an alias for it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is aburi? Is the fish cooked or still raw?
proposals.menuLine: Aburi Otoro Nigiri, Torched, Fresh Wasabi, Sea Salt

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list. It is printed as 'Binchotan-Grilled' or 'over Binchotan' on omakase, yakitori and robata menus. Binchotan is Japanese white oak charcoal, fired until it is almost pure carbon. It burns very hot, steady, clean and nearly smokeless, so it chars the surface without the smoky taste of wood or briquettes. Guests ask what the charcoal is and how this differs from Grilled, the L1 card. Only a senior server answers that well, and it is specialist, so it is a Chef word. No card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is binchotan, and how is that different from just grilled?
proposals.menuLine: Binchotan-Grilled Chicken Thigh, Tare, Charred Scallion, Shichimi

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list. Menus also print it as Hay-Roasted. Lamb, chicken, potatoes, eggs or cheese are cooked inside, or smoked over, smoldering hay. The method is old French farmhouse cooking revived on Nordic and New American tasting menus, and it gives a sweet, grassy, toasted smoke. Guests ask whether they eat the hay and how it differs from Smoked (smoldering wood, L1). It is rare and needs a sentence on the near neighbor, so it is a Chef word. No card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: Hay-smoked? Do I eat the hay, and is it different from regular smoked?
proposals.menuLine: Hay-Smoked Lamb Loin, Sunchoke, Black Garlic, Lamb Jus

dispositions.reason: The challenger is right that by the standard it is a Level III word. It now appears on most hearth and wood-fire menus, one sentence explains it, and it carries the same weight as A la Plancha and Salt-Baked (L3), not Koji-Aged or Ikejime (L4). This run builds Level 4 only, so the word is DROPPED from this roster rather than moved, and Binchotan-Grilled takes its live-fire slot at Level 4. Carry Ember-Roasted (aliases Ash-Roasted, Coal-Roasted) into the next Level III run.

The challenger is right. Compressed watermelon, melon and cucumber have spread from tasting menus to ordinary upscale salad sections. The word needs one sentence but is neither rare nor specialist, so it is Level III by the standard, alongside Lacquered. This run builds Level 4 only, so it is DROPPED from this roster rather than moved, and Hay-Smoked takes its slot. Carry it into the next Level III run.

Added at Level 4 as 'Binchotan-Grilled', the method form menus print, which fits a section of cooking verbs. It is a specialist Japanese fire with a real near-neighbor contrast against Grilled and Smoked. No card or alias covers it.
Added at Level 4 with Hay-Roasted noted as the menu variant. It is a rare tasting-menu method with a real near-neighbor contrast against Smoked. Nothing in the deck covers it.

challenges.because: It is now standard on every hearth-driven or wood-fire menu, not just tasting menus. A Level III server meets it most weeks, and one sentence covers it: cooked in or against the coals, so the skin chars and the inside steams. It is the same weight as the deck's other Level III method words, A la Plancha and Salt-Baked, not a rare word like Koji-Aged or Ikejime. Menus also print it as Ash-Roasted or Coal-Roasted, so carry those as aliases.

Compressed watermelon, cucumber and melon have spread from modernist tasting menus to ordinary upscale salad sections, so a fine-dining server sees the word all the time. It needs a sentence (vacuum-sealed so the air collapses, making it dense and glassy), but it is not rare or specialist. That is Level III fine-dining vocabulary by the standard, the same tier as Lacquered.

missing: Binchotan [4] (printed as 'Binchotan-Grilled' on omakase, yakitori and robata menus. Guests ask what the white charcoal is and why it differs from Grilled: very hot, clean and nearly smokeless. The deck has no card or alias for it.)

Hay-Smoked [4] (menus also print it as Hay-Roasted. Lamb, chicken, potatoes or cheese are cooked or smoked over or inside smoldering hay, a classical French and Nordic tasting-menu word. Guests ask whether they eat the hay and how it differs from Smoked.)
sections.note: I propose five Level 4 words, all checked against everyCard terms and aliases (searched for papillote, vessie, kombu, aburi, ember, cendre, compress, cuit, hay and others). None of the Lexicon candidates belongs to this section, so no proposal carries a slug. I left several words out on purpose. En Vessie and Barigoule are preparations, not methods; that section already holds En Papillote and En Croûte. Flambé, Butter-Basted and Cold-Smoked are Level 2 or 3, which this run does not want. Brûléed and Lacto-Fermented are near-variants of Crème Brûlée and Fermented. Binchotan and Robata are a fuel and a grill style, closer to the language or pantry sections. Hay-Smoked or Hay-Roasted is a possible sixth Level 4 word if the owner wants one, but it shows up on fewer menus than the five above. One owner call to flag: memory records live-fire doctrine as the owner's decision, so Ember-Roasted (and Aburi, if fire wording counts) should be checked against that before a card is written.

proposals.reason: This is the prize of the wild-game season. Scottish red grouse is shot from the Glorious Twelfth (12 August) and flown to top American kitchens for a few weeks each autumn. It is rare, short-seasoned and expensive. It eats very differently from the farmed birds the deck already teaches (Quail, Pheasant, Guinea Hen, Squab): dark, gamey and close to liver in flavor. A senior server has to explain that it is truly wild, why it is served pink and how strong it tastes. This card also carries the wild-versus-farmed lesson for the other game birds. The deck has no grouse under any term or alias.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is the grouse actually wild, and how gamey is it compared with the squab?
proposals.menuLine: Roast Scottish Red Grouse, bread sauce, game chips, blackberries, liver toast

proposals.reason: Hare is a different animal from the deck's Rabbit (Level 2). It is wild, dark-fleshed and strongly flavored, where farmed rabbit is pale and mild, and diners who know food test servers on that difference. In the US it appears mostly as imported Scottish hare in autumn: in the classical lièvre à la royale, and on Italian menus as lepre (pappardelle alla lepre). It is rare, specialist and deeply classical, which is the Level 4 standard. The deck has no hare, lepre or lièvre under any alias.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is hare just rabbit? Why is it so much darker?
proposals.menuLine: Pappardelle alla Lepre, slow-braised hare ragù, juniper, Parmigiano

proposals.reason: The rooster's comb is braised until gelatinous, then often fried crisp. It is a classical garnish (financière, the Piedmontese finanziera) that tasting menus now serve as a nose-to-tail bite. It is the offal a nervous guest is most likely to ask about, and the server needs the honest description this section is built for: soft and collagen-rich, like the skin of a braised trotter. It is rare on menus and needs explaining, so it sits at Level 4. It is not in the deck under any term or alias (crête de coq, rooster comb).
proposals.guestsAsk: What exactly is a cockscomb, and what is the texture like?
proposals.menuLine: Crispy Cockscomb, chicken-liver mousse, pickled shallot, sherry gastrique

proposals.reason: This is the North American line of the French Bresse chicken (poulet bleu). Fine-dining menus name the bird to justify a whole roast chicken for two at a luxury price. The server must explain the breed (blue feet, white feathers, red comb), why the meat is firmer and more flavorful, and how it relates to Poulet de Bresse, which cannot be imported. It is also the bird the top rooms use for the classical 'en vessie' preparation, which is where a guest who knows Bocuse meets it. A specialist product word the deck lacks under any alias (Bresse, Poulet Bleu).
proposals.guestsAsk: What makes a blue foot chicken different, and is it the same as a Bresse chicken?
proposals.menuLine: Roast Blue Foot Chicken for Two, morels, vin jaune, pommes purée

proposals.reason: This is the deeply classical offal of the French bistro (cervelle de veau au beurre noir) and of nose-to-tail menus, printed as Calf's Brains, Veal Brains or Cervelle de Veau. Without it the section's offal side is thin, and it is the organ a nervous guest most needs described honestly: very soft and custardy, mild and creamy, usually poached and then seared in brown butter with capers. A senior server also has to answer the safety question calmly: US rules bar brain only from cattle 30 months and older, so these are young calves' brains. Rare on menus and needs explaining, so it sits at Level 4. Neither Sweetbreads nor any other card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What do brains actually taste like, and are they safe to eat?
proposals.menuLine: Cervelle de Veau, brown butter, capers, lemon, parsley, grilled country bread

dispositions.reason: Dropped. American menus print the preparation (en Vessie, demi-deuil) on a Bresse or blue foot bird far more often than they print the word Poularde, and the bladder question belongs to Preparations. The guest who meets that dish is now served by the Blue Foot Chicken card, whose reason names the en vessie link.

Dropping Poularde does not mean the section needs another fattened-bird word. Capon is a holiday special or a broth (brodo di cappone) on a few Italian menus, not a word a captain is routinely tested on, and it takes one sentence to explain (a castrated, fattened rooster). The fifth slot goes to offal, which this section is short of.

Wild woodcock cannot legally be sold in the US, so it reaches only a handful of rooms as imported Scottish birds for a few days a year. That makes it a textbook word more than a menu word. Grouse already carries the lessons of the wild autumn game bird and of eating game pink. The 'roasted with the entrails, served on toast' story is better kept as a note under Grouse than as a fifth game bird.

The partridge on American menus is mostly farmed red-legged partridge. It sits beside the deck's Quail and Pheasant in flavor and needs little more explanation than they do, so it does not reach the Level 4 standard. The 'how does it compare with grouse' question is answered on the Grouse card. If it is wanted at all, it is a Level 3 word for a later run.

Wild-shot waterfowl cannot be sold commercially in the US, so a menu's 'Mallard' is usually a farm-raised mallard-type bird. Guests asking 'is it wild?' would get a confusing answer. Duck is already covered by Duck Breast (Magret) and Moulard, and the wild-versus-farmed lesson sits on Grouse.

Added as the fifth word. It is the most classical offal missing from the section, and the honest description it needs, together with the safety answer a nervous guest asks for, is exactly what the section blurb asks for.

Calf's Brains fills the one offal slot more classically. Lamb fries are regional (Kentucky, the West) or appear as animelles at a few French rooms. The usual alias, Rocky Mountain Oysters, is bull calf testicles, not lamb, so the card would teach a confusion a guest could catch. It is held for a later run with that distinction written in.

These appear mainly on Chinese menus and on a small number of tasting menus. Duck Hearts already teaches the small duck-offal bite, and Beef Tongue teaches tongue as meat, so the remaining explanation (a small bone in the middle) is a line, not a Level 4 card. The cap of five goes to words a fine-dining captain meets more often.

challenges.because: American menus almost never print it. The rooms that serve the Bocuse dish print the preparation, 'en Vessie', on a Bresse or blue foot chicken ('Poulet en Vessie', 'Volaille en Vessie'). Guests ask about the bladder, not the bird, and that question belongs to Preparations. In this section the fattened bird an American guest actually meets is Capon (Cappone at Christmas, tortellini in brodo di cappone), so teach that word instead. 'Demi-deuil' is likewise a preparation, not an animal.

missing: Woodcock [4]: the most classical wild bird on an autumn game menu (bécasse). It is roasted with the entrails in and served on toast, and guests who know game will ask if that is true. No card or alias covers it.
Partridge [4]: grey-legged or red-legged partridge (perdrix, pernice) on autumn game menus beside grouse. It is milder than grouse, and guests ask how it compares with quail and pheasant.
Mallard [4]: wild duck, printed as Mallard, Wild Duck or Teal. It is lean, dark and gamey against the farmed Duck Breast and Moulard. 'Is it wild?' is the guest's question.
Capon [4]: the castrated, fattened rooster on holiday and Italian menus (Cappone). It replaces Poularde as this section's fattened-bird word.
Calf's Brains [4]: printed as Cervelle de Veau or Brains with brown butter and capers. It is the offal a nervous guest most needs described honestly. No card or alias covers it.
Lamb Fries [4]: lamb testicles, printed as Lamb Fries, Animelles or Rocky Mountain Oysters. Guests always ask what they are, and the server needs the honest answer this section is built for.
Duck Tongues [4]: on tasting and modern Chinese menus, fried or glazed. They are a small bone-in bite that guests ask about. The deck's Beef Tongue card does not cover them.
sections.note: I read roster.meats.brief.json and searched everyCard for every term and alias. None of the five words is taught under any term, alias or spelling variant. No Lexicon slug is given for any of them: none of the 31 candidates in the brief is about poultry, game or offal. Other Level 4 words I considered but left out: Woodcock (very rarely sold in the US), Pressed Duck and Civet (preparations, so they likely belong in the preparations section, not this one), and veal kidney and calf's brain (Rognons and Cervelle). The kidney and brain words are more honestly Level 3, and this run wants Level 4 only. Partridge and Capon are also Level 3 at most.

proposals.reason: The classical showpiece of the charcuterie board: a forcemeat of pork, veal or game, often with an inlay of foie gras, duck or pistachio, baked inside a decorated pastry crust. Once it cools, aspic is poured into the gap between meat and crust, and it is served cold in thick slices. It is back on refined American French menus and boards, and guests who know food ask about the jelly layer and whether it is served warm. I checked the deck. En Croûte (fd_0338) teaches only the hot technique, with a salmon en croûte line and a Wellington gloss. Pâté (fd_0073) teaches the baked loaf. Neither card names this cold, jellied, crusted piece, so it belongs here and not in preparations.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is the pâté en croûte served warm, and what is the clear layer between the crust and the meat?
proposals.menuLine: Pâté en croûte of duck and pork, foie gras and pistachio center, cornichons, whole-grain mustard

proposals.reason: The white sausage of France: finely ground pork, veal or chicken bound with milk or cream, egg and sometimes bread. It is poached and then browned gently in butter. It is the French Christmas sausage and is often truffled (boudin blanc truffé) on holiday and tasting menus. It is the counterpart to Boudin Noir (fd_0312), which names it only in a notThis line and does not teach it. Guests ask whether it contains blood, and whether it is the Cajun boudin. It is neither.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is in a white sausage? Is there blood in it, like the boudin noir?
proposals.menuLine: Truffled boudin blanc, pommes purée, sauce Périgueux

proposals.reason: Mallorca's soft cured pork sausage, heavy with pimentón, which spreads like a paste. Sobrassada de Mallorca is protected. It is a fixture of Spanish tapas and fine-dining Spanish menus, usually on toast with honey. Guests always set it against 'Nduja (fd_0081), so the server must explain the difference: it is Spanish, not Calabrian, and paprika-sweet and smoky, not chile-hot. It is a separate product, not a spelling of anything in the deck. The Catalan spelling Sobrassada goes on the card as an alias.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that like 'nduja? Is it spicy?
proposals.menuLine: Sobrasada toast, wildflower honey, Marcona almonds

proposals.reason: A large Emilian pork sausage made soft and rich with salted pork rind. It is simmered for hours and served hot in thick slices, traditionally with lentils at New Year, and it appears on winter and seasonal menus at refined Italian restaurants. It fills this section's cooked-versus-raw line, because it is a salume you never slice raw. The deck mentions it only in a pairings line on a pantry card and teaches it nowhere. Its twin Zampone (the same filling stuffed into a boned pig's trotter) belongs in this card's notThis, because guests ask which is which and it rarely appears on American menus by itself.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is cotechino cured like salami, or is it cooked? What makes it so soft?
proposals.menuLine: Cotechino, braised Umbrian lentils, salsa verde, mostarda di Cremona

proposals.reason: The French sausage of pork chitterlings and stomach, cut in strips and packed into a casing. It comes from Troyes and Lyon, is grilled and served with mustard and frites, and has a strong barnyard smell that guests should hear about before they order. Bistros print the AAAAA seal of the andouillette society beside it. It is the word guests test a server on, because the deck teaches Andouille (fd_0064), the smoked Cajun sausage, and the two share only a root. Andouillette is a different product and not a spelling of Andouille. The server who says 'not the Cajun one, and here is what it is' saves a returned plate.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that the Cajun sausage? What is it actually made of?
proposals.menuLine: Andouillette de Troyes AAAAA, grilled, Dijon mustard sauce, frites

dispositions.reason: Dropped. It is accurate and distinct from Culatello, but American menus rarely print it outside a few salumi bars, and it is weaker on the floor than the five that stand. It fits best as a notThis line on Culatello (fd_0309), the next time that card is edited.

Dropped. Cecina de León is real and the Lexicon holds it (cecina-de-leon), but American menus print it far less often than Sobrasada, which takes the one Spanish slot. The unsmoked-versus-smoked beef contrast can live as a notThis line on Bresaola (fd_0079).

Dropped. It is the closest of the five to a word the deck already teaches (Lomo, fd_0070, the same whole cured loin). The proposer's alias fallback is rejected too: the Lomo gist says the loin is rubbed with smoked paprika, and Lonza has none, so the alias would teach something false. The Italian loin goes in as a notThis line on Lomo instead.
Added at Level 4. It is on French bistro menus, guests test servers on it, and the deck's Andouille (fd_0064) is the trap it guards against. It is a separate product, not a spelling variant.
Added at Level 4. Boudin Noir (fd_0312) names it only in its notThis line and does not teach it. Truffled boudin blanc is a holiday and tasting-menu fixture.

Added after the requested check. En Croûte (fd_0338) teaches the hot pastry-wrap technique with a salmon line and a Wellington gloss, and links the recipe without naming the cold, jellied charcuterie piece. Pâté (fd_0073) teaches the baked loaf. The named dish is its own word on refined menus. The Lexicon holds it as pate-en-croute, but the brief's candidates do not list it, so no lexiconSlug is set.

The deck already teaches the distinction. The Ballotine card (fd_0228) carries a trap answering 'cold loaf of poached poultry set in its own jelly' with 'That is a galantine', and that covers the guest's question. Galantine is also rarely printed on current American menus. If it ever earns a card, it belongs beside Ballotine in preparations, not on the board.

It is rare on American menus, even at the top end, and fine-dining guests seldom ask about it. The jellied cold-meat idea is already taught by Head Cheese (fd_0311). The Lexicon folds it into its French-hams entry rather than giving it its own entry, which supports leaving it out.

Not given a separate card. It rarely appears on American menus without Cotechino beside it, and the guest's question is 'which one is which'. That is answered by a notThis line on the new Cotechino card (same filling, stuffed into a boned trotter). It is not an alias, because it is a different casing and a different product.

On American menus it appears almost only as an unnamed ingredient inside XO sauce and superior stock, not as a named item on the board, so a server meets it as a pantry component and not as charcuterie. It loses the five slots to words that are actually printed, and if it ever earns a card, it belongs with the sauce or pantry words.

missing: Andouillette [4]: the French chitterling and tripe sausage from Troyes and Lyon, grilled with mustard on bistro menus. It is the word guests test a server on, because the deck teaches Andouille (fd_0064) and the two are nothing alike. 'Is that the Cajun sausage?' 'No, and here is what it is.'

Boudin Blanc [4]: the white veal, pork or chicken sausage bound with milk, often truffled on holiday and tasting menus. It is the counterpart to Boudin Noir (fd_0312), which the deck already teaches, and no card names it.

Galantine [4]: deboned poultry or meat, stuffed, rolled, poached and served cold in its own aspic. It belongs to the charcuterie board, not the hot line. It is not Ballotine (fd_0228, preparations), which is served hot, and guests ask what separates the two. Give it its own card and set it against Ballotine.

Pâté en Croûte [4]: the classical pâté in a pastry crust with a jelly layer, revived on refined American menus and boards. Check first that En Croûte (fd_0338) does not already gloss it. If that card teaches only the technique, the named charcuterie piece belongs here.
Jambon Persillé [4]: Burgundy's ham set in parsley aspic, on French bistro and wine-bar menus at the top end. A cold cooked ham that the deck does not teach under any name.

Zampone [4]: Cotechino's twin, the same rind-rich filling stuffed into a boned pig's trotter and served at New Year with lentils. If Cotechino is accepted, either teach Zampone beside it or add it to that card, because guests ask which one is which.

Jinhua Ham [4]: China's great dry-cured ham, printed on fine-dining Chinese menus and behind XO sauce and superior stock. It is the one cured meat in this section outside Europe and America that a senior server is asked about.
sections.note: All five are Level 4 only, as this run asks; none is Level 3. I checked each word against everyCard and the live floor-deck.json (336 cards). None is a card term or an alias. Several stronger words are already taught elsewhere, so I dropped them: Pâté en Croûte is a variant of En Croûte (preparations), Torchon is in preparations, and Morcilla and Jamón de Bellota are close variants of existing cards. Lonza is the only borderline case; its reason sets out the fallback of adding it as a Lomo alias. Mortadella, Jambon de Bayonne, Saucisson Sec and Boudin Blanc are real gaps in this section, but they belong at Level 2 or 3, which this run excludes. No Lexicon candidate fits this section, so no lexiconSlug is given.

proposals.reason: The deeply classical name for thick, round medallions cut from the narrow middle of the beef tenderloin. It is still printed on refined French and fine-dining steak menus, most often as Tournedos Rossini (foie gras, black truffle, Madeira, crouton). The deck holds Tenderloin (alias Filet Mignon) at I and Chateaubriand at III, but no card or alias names the tournedos, and the word appears nowhere in the deck's text. A guest who knows food tests the server on how it differs from a filet mignon (which part of the muscle, how thick, how it is tied and served) and on what makes it Rossini. That precise answer, together with the classical garnish, is Chef-level knowledge. No challenge was raised against it.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is a tournedos just a filet mignon, and what makes it Rossini?
proposals.menuLine: Tournedos Rossini, seared foie gras, black truffle, Madeira sauce, brioche crouton

proposals.reason: The prized fresh Ibérico cut from where the shoulder meets the loin: thick, deeply marbled and grilled pink like a beef steak. Guests and menus compare it to a ribeye. Spanish-led and tasting menus in American cities print it by name, often as Presa de Bellota, and it costs accordingly. It is a different muscle from Secreto Ibérico (fd_0316, the deck's only Level IV cut), so it is not an alias or a spelling variant. The challenger's argument stands that the section can carry one more Ibérico card but not two, and Presa is the one printed more often. The earlier run kept both siblings off the deck when the owner had not yet asked for a heavier Chef level. That has now changed: this section holds a single Level IV card. This is a rare specialist product with a breed, feed and pricing story a captain must own, the same tier as Secreto.
proposals.guestsAsk: Pork served pink? How is the presa different from the secreto, and why is it priced like a steak?
proposals.menuLine: Grilled Presa Ibérica de Bellota, Ibérico-fat potatoes, pimentón, sherry vinegar

proposals.reason: The Tuscan porterhouse: cut about three fingers thick, traditionally from Chianina cattle, grilled over wood, served only rare and dressed with olive oil after it leaves the fire. It is sold by weight for the table. Italian fine-dining rooms and Italian steakhouses in American cities print it by name. The Porterhouse and T-Bone card (fd_0096) teaches the anatomy, but the deck never names the bistecca (no 'Fiorentina' or 'Chianina' anywhere in it). The word carries a rule set of its own that a guest tests the server on: why it cannot be cooked past rare, why it is for two, and why it is priced by the kilo. That is more than a translation, the same reason Chateaubriand stands as its own card beside Tenderloin rather than as an alias (unlike Côte de Boeuf, which adds nothing to the Ribeye card). Deeply classical and specialist, so it is Level IV. It belongs in Meat Cuts because it names a cut taken a specific way, as Chateaubriand does.
proposals.guestsAsk: Why can the Fiorentina only be cooked rare, and why is it priced by weight and for two?
proposals.menuLine: Bistecca alla Fiorentina for two, 40 oz dry-aged porterhouse, Tuscan olive oil, rosemary, lemon, priced by weight

proposals.reason: The curly-coated Hungarian 'woolly pig' (Hungarian spelling Mangalica), a lard breed whose fat is unusually high, soft and quick to melt. Chef-driven and tasting menus print it by name on chops, coppa and lardo, and its price is well above Berkshire. Breed words already sit in this section (Wagyu, fd_0107), so it belongs here. Heritage Breed (fd_0297, language) teaches the general idea and names only Berkshire, and the deck never names Mangalitsa. A guest who reads it asks what it is, why the fat looks the way it does, and why it costs more. It is rare and specialist, the pork counterpart of a Wagyu question one level up.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is a Mangalitsa pig, and why is it so fatty and so much more expensive than Berkshire?
proposals.menuLine: Mangalitsa Pork Chop, bone-in, charred cabbage, apple mostarda, cider jus

dispositions.reason: Dropped. One more Ibérico card in this section is the most it can carry, and Presa is the one printed more often and the one guests compare to a steak. Data fix for the writer: the shipped Secreto Ibérico card (fd_0316) names neither sibling, although the earlier reconciler promised it would. Its body (why or notThis) should name Pluma, the feather-shaped cut at the front tip of the loin, and should point to the new Presa card, so the guest who asks about all three in one breath gets an answer.

Agreed that it is a Sous Chef-tier specialist-cut word, alongside Coulotte and Chateaubriand. American rooms mostly print 'lamb loin' or 'rabbit loin', and the Rabbit card (fd_0058) already teaches the fast loin and braised legs. This run builds only Level IV, so Saddle leaves the list. It can be weighed again in a Level III run, but the earlier run already dropped it as a book word.

Agreed. It sits in the nose-to-tail tier with Tripe (fd_0305) and Sweetbreads (fd_0054) at III. It is no rarer or more classical than tripe, and a server at any French bistro or nose-to-tail room meets it regularly. Level III is not wanted in this run, so it leaves the Chef list.

dispositions.term: Pig Trotter (challenge: rename to Pig's Trotter)
dispositions.reason: Accepted for the record: menus print 'Pig's Trotter' or 'Pied de Cochon'. If a Level III run takes the card, it should carry that term with Pied de Cochon and Pig's Feet as aliases, so the Ham Hock trap (fd_0089) and the tripe text that mention trotters point at it. It is not on this run's list because of the level move above.

Added at Level IV. It is printed by name on chef-driven and tasting menus and is asked about for its fat and its price. The deck never names it (Heritage Breed fd_0297 names only Berkshire), and Wagyu sets the precedent for a breed card in this section.

Wrong section, and thin on American menus. Hogget names an animal's age, not where on the animal a cut comes from, so it parallels Poussin (fd_0057), which lives in the meats section, not this one. It also appears mainly on British and a handful of farm-to-table menus, below every word kept here. It can be raised in the meats roster if that section has room.

Added at Level IV in this section. It names a cut taken a specific way (thickness, breed, rare only, sold by weight), as Chateaubriand does, and that is why it is a card and not an alias of Porterhouse and T-Bone. Its conventions are exactly what a guest tests the server on. The deck never names it.

dispositions.term: Côte de Boeuf [alias on Ribeye fd_0090] (missing)
dispositions.reason: Accepted as an alias, not a card, and not counted in this list. It is the bone-in rib steak for two that the Ribeye card already teaches under Cowboy Steak and Tomahawk. The earlier run asked for it and it was never added (the deck text holds no 'Côte de'). Data fix for the writer: add 'Côte de Boeuf' to fd_0090's aliases.

challenges.because: The deck can carry one more Ibérico card in this section, not two. The earlier roster run already ruled against both siblings as separate cards (roster.run.json, cuts dispositions: 'Presa [4] and Pluma [4]'), because two more would put three of the section's Level IV cards on one pig. Of the two, Presa is the one American Spanish-led and tasting menus print more often, and it is the cut guests compare to a steak. Keep Presa and name Pluma inside the Secreto Ibérico card (fd_0316). That reconciler promised the Secreto card would name its siblings and the shipped card still names neither, so fix that whichever one is kept.

This word was already weighed and graded Level III in the earlier roster run, then dropped as a book word: American rooms, fine dining included, mostly print 'lamb loin' or 'rabbit loin'. The reason given here, loin cooked fast and pink with the legs braised, is already taught by the Rabbit card (fd_0058: 'kitchens often cook the loin briefly and braise the legs'), so a new card would add only the anatomy word. That is specialist-cut vocabulary in the same tier as Coulotte and Chateaubriand (III), not Chef.

This is the nose-to-tail tier. Tripe (fd_0305) and Sweetbreads (fd_0054) sit at III, and Bone Marrow and Beef Tongue sit at II. A trotter takes the same honest sentence to a nervous guest that tripe does, and a server at any nose-to-tail or French-bistro room meets it regularly. It is not rarer or more classical than tripe, so it does not belong at Chef.

Menus print 'Pig's Trotter' (or 'Pied de Cochon' at French rooms), not 'Pig Trotter'. Keep Pied de Cochon and Pig's Feet as aliases so the Ham Hock card's trap (fd_0089) and the tripe text that mention trotters point at the card.

missing: Mangalitsa [4]: the curly-coated 'woolly pig' printed by name on chef-driven and tasting menus for its unusually high, soft fat. Guests ask what it is and why it costs more than Berkshire. The Heritage Breed card (fd_0297) teaches the idea and names only Berkshire, and Wagyu sits in this section as a breed card, so a breed word belongs here

Hogget [4]: a sheep between one and two years old, older than lamb and younger than mutton, printed on farm-to-table and British-leaning fine-dining menus. Guests always ask whether it is lamb or mutton and how gamy it is. No card or alias names it

Bistecca alla Fiorentina [4]: the Tuscan thick-cut porterhouse, traditionally Chianina beef, sold by weight for the table and served only rare. It is on Italian fine-dining menus in American cities, and guests ask why it can't be cooked past rare and why it is for two. The Porterhouse and T-Bone card (fd_0096) does not teach the name. If the owner calls it a preparation, it goes to that section instead

Côte de Boeuf [alias on Ribeye fd_0090, not a new card]: the earlier roster run asked for it as an alias and it was never added. It is printed on French and steakhouse menus for the bone-in rib steak for two
sections.note: This run proposes five Level IV words for Meat Cuts and no Level III words. None of the brief's Lexicon candidates belongs to this section, so no proposal carries a lexiconSlug. I checked all five against everyCard (terms and aliases). None appears there, and none appears in the section's source module except the trotter, which is only a distractor line on the Ham Hock card (fd_0089). I deliberately left out words that the deck already teaches under another name: Côte de Boeuf and Entrecôte are covered by Ribeye (with its Cowboy and Tomahawk aliases), Deckle is ambiguous with Ribeye Cap and Spinalis, Kobe and A5 are covered by Wagyu, Vacío and Entraña are covered by Flank and Skirt, Noisette clashes with the Beurre Noisette alias on Brown Butter, and Pork Collar clashes with Coppa. Breeds such as Mangalitsa belong in Meats or Language, not here. If the owner wants fewer Ibérico cards, Presa can be dropped and Pluma kept.

proposals.reason: The caviar name printed on almost every American caviar service, and the one a captain is tested on most. The deck teaches Caviar only as a category (salt-cured sturgeon eggs). Osetra (also spelled Ossetra or Oscietra) is a particular sturgeon: medium beads, amber to brown, nutty and briny. To explain it a server needs the species, bead size, colour and why it costs what it costs next to Kaluga, Beluga and the farmed hybrids. That is specialist product knowledge, which makes it Level IV. No card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What's the difference between the osetra and the kaluga, and why is one so much more?
proposals.menuLine: Osetra Caviar, 30 g, potato blini, crème fraîche, chive

proposals.reason: The European flat oyster (Ostrea edulis). It is named for the Belon river in Brittany and is raised in Maine as Maine Belons. It is a different species from the cupped oysters the Oysters card teaches, and it is the raw bar's connoisseur test: a round, flat shell, an intense coppery or metallic finish, the top price on the list, and a short season. The server has to warn the guest about that finish before the plate lands. It is printed by name on serious raw-bar and fine-dining lists, and it is no alias of Oysters.
proposals.guestsAsk: Why is the Belon so much more expensive, and why does it taste like metal?
proposals.menuLine: Maine Belon Oysters, half dozen, champagne mignonette

proposals.reason: The Maine rock crab, renamed by fine-dining kitchens in the 1990s. It is still printed by name in the crab salads, tartlets and crudos of refined New York and New England menus. A guest who knows food asks what it is and how it differs from blue or Dungeness crab, and the server needs the story: a once-discarded bycatch, hand-picked into delicate, sweet, pink-flecked meat. Blue Crab and Soft-Shell Crab teach the Chesapeake swimmer only, and no card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is peekytoe crab, and is it the same as blue crab or Dungeness?
proposals.menuLine: Peekytoe Crab, avocado, green apple, yuzu, crispy rice

proposals.reason: The tiny wild bay scallop of Nantucket and the Cape. It has a short winter season, is far sweeter than the sea scallop, costs well above it, and appears on New England and New York fine-dining menus by name for a few weeks a year. The Scallops card teaches the large sea scallop and carries no bay-scallop alias. Explaining this one takes the species, the size, the season and the price, which puts it at Level IV as specialist seasonal product knowledge rather than a variant of Scallops.
proposals.guestsAsk: Why are these scallops so small, and why do they cost more than the big ones?
proposals.menuLine: Nantucket Bay Scallops, brown butter, celery root, black truffle

proposals.reason: The French menu name for red mullet (rouget barbet), a small rosy Mediterranean fish central to classical French and Provençal cooking. It is served as crisp-skinned fillets with a rich, almost shellfish-like flavour that comes from its crustacean diet. Refined French menus print it with no English gloss. Guests confuse it with Red Snapper (a card), and its fine pin bones are worth a word to the guest. It is the one finfish in this roster, deeply classical and specialist, and nothing in the deck covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What kind of fish is rouget, is it like snapper, and are there bones?
proposals.menuLine: Rouget, saffron fennel, olive, bouillabaisse jus

dispositions.reason: No challenge raised. The proposal stands: caviar grades are the most printed and most tested Level IV word in the section, and Osetra is not an alias of Caviar.
No challenge raised. The proposal stands: it is a separate species from the Oysters card, with a real connoisseur's flavour warning that a server must give.
No challenge raised. The proposal stands and keeps one finfish in a list that would otherwise hold only shellfish and roe.

Dropped to keep the section at five. On these menus it is mostly a West Coast tasting-menu and Chinese-banquet word, and Peekytoe Crab and Nantucket Bay Scallops are printed by name more often at the fine-dining American restaurants this deck serves. It stays a good later candidate, especially because guests confuse it with the Abalone Mushroom card.

Dropped to keep the section at five. It is a real and growing luxury prawn, but it appears mainly on Spanish-leaning menus and less often than the five kept. The guest's 'eat the head' question also overlaps what a server already says for Langoustine and head-on Shrimp.

Added. It is printed by name in refined crab dishes across New York and New England, guests ask what it is and how it differs from blue or Dungeness, and Blue Crab and Soft-Shell Crab do not cover it.
Added. It is a named, seasonal, premium wild product that the Scallops card (sea scallop, no aliases) does not teach, and it is printed by name on fine-dining winter menus.
A real luxury, but it is printed mainly at Spanish and a few Pacific Northwest tasting counters, more rarely than the five kept. With a cap of five, it loses on the menu-frequency signal.
It lives almost entirely on sushi and omakase menus as sashimi or crudo, and much less on the fine-dining American menus this deck trains for. It is outranked by the five kept under the cap.

The Roe card already teaches roe 'cooked whole in the sac', which is the shad roe preparation. What remains is a few weeks of regional seasonality on fewer and fewer menus, so it is weaker than the five kept.
An omakase-counter word (monkfish liver). It is rarely printed on non-Japanese fine-dining menus, and it loses to the five kept under the cap of five.
A high-end omakase fish, almost never printed outside a sushi counter's list. It is narrower than the five kept, so it is not added under the cap.

missing: Percebes [4]: gooseneck barnacles, the Galician and Pacific Northwest luxury on Spanish-leaning and tasting menus. Guests ask 'what is that, and how do I eat it?' (twist off the leathery sleeve, eat the pink stalk). No card or alias covers it.

Geoduck [4]: the giant Pacific clam, pronounced 'gooey-duck', served as sashimi or crudo on West Coast and omakase menus. Guests ask how to say it and what part they are eating. The Clams card (Littlenecks, Quahogs, Steamers) does not cover it.

Shad Roe [4]: the East Coast spring classic, a pair of roe sacs seared in brown butter, often with bacon, on the menu for a few weeks a year. The Roe card is generic, and nothing teaches the seasonal shad dish a guest who knows food will order and quiz the server on.

Nantucket Bay Scallops [4]: the tiny, very sweet wild bay scallop with a short winter season, priced far above sea scallops and printed by name on New England and New York fine-dining menus. The Scallops card covers the sea scallop and gives no alias for the bay scallop.

Peekytoe Crab [4]: the Maine rock crab that the fine-dining kitchens of the 1990s renamed, printed by name in crab salads and tartlets. Guests ask what it is and how it differs from blue or Dungeness crab. Blue Crab and Soft-Shell Crab do not cover it.
Ankimo [4]: monkfish liver, steamed and called the foie gras of the sea, found on omakase and fine-dining menus. The Monkfish card (Anglerfish, Lotte) teaches the tail only, so the liver is untaught.

Kinmedai [4]: golden-eye snapper, the prized red-skinned deep-water fish served aburi (skin seared) at high-end omakase counters. Guests ask whether it is the same as red snapper, and it is not, so it belongs beside the Snapper card without being an alias of it.
sections.note: No Lexicon candidate in the brief is a fish or shellfish term, so lexiconSlug is left empty for all five. I checked everyCard: none of these words, or any variant spelling (Ossetra, Oscietra, Carabineros, Red Mullet), appears as a term or alias. "Abalone Mushroom" names the fungus, not the shellfish. Other honest Level IV options I held back so the section stays at five: Percebes (gooseneck barnacles; Spanish-leaning menus, rarer in the US), Kinmedai (golden-eye snapper; mainly omakase), Shirako (cod milt; omakase) and Ankimo (monkfish liver; close to the Monkfish card). The section also lacks several common Level II/III words, such as Octopus, Squid, Hamachi, Ikura, Toro, Sablefish, Razor Clams, Spot Prawns, John Dory and Dorade. They are outside this Level IV-only run but worth a future Level II/III pass.

proposals.reason: The spring white truffle (Tuber borchii, also sold as marzuolo). Fine-dining menus print it from about January to April, after the Alba season closes, and it is the truffle most often passed off as Alba. The White Truffle card (fd_0321) does not name it under any alias or in its text, so the deck never teaches this distinction. A captain must know it is a different species: smaller, sharper and more garlicky, and a fraction of the price. That is specialist knowledge for a senior server, so it sits at Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that the same as the white truffle from Alba, and why is it so much cheaper?
proposals.menuLine: Hand-cut tagliolini, cultured butter, shaved bianchetto truffle

proposals.reason: Corn smut (Ustilago maydis), a fungus that swells corn kernels into silvery-black lobes. Menus also print it as cuitlacoche or as 'Mexican truffle'. It is a regular at modern Mexican and progressive American restaurants. It fits the section blurb's 'what a truffle is and is not' exactly: it is a prized fungus but not a truffle, and not a mushroom in the usual sense. It takes a confident sentence to explain without putting the guest off. No card, alias or card text in the deck covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is huitlacoche, and is it actually a truffle?
proposals.menuLine: Blue corn tetela, huitlacoche, Oaxaca cheese, salsa macha

proposals.reason: Not a species of its own. A mold (Hypomyces lactifluorum) parasitizes a Russula or Lactifluus host, turns it bright red-orange and firms it, and leaves a faint seafood smell. It is printed on late-summer and fall wild-mushroom menus. The server has to explain the parasitism and has to answer the shellfish-allergy question correctly: the name refers to color and smell only, and it contains no shellfish. That is specialist product knowledge. No card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: Does it have lobster in it? I have a shellfish allergy.
proposals.menuLine: Seared halibut, lobster mushrooms, sweet corn, chervil

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list. It is a small wild winter mushroom (Craterellus tubaeformis, also printed 'winter chanterelle'), with a hollow yellow stem under a thin brown cap. It is printed on winter menus when golden chanterelles are gone. It sits between two cards the deck already teaches: it is not the golden Chanterelle (fd_0141), and it is in the same genus as the Black Trumpet (fd_0140) but not the same mushroom. Neither card carries it as an alias. Owning that three-way distinction is the senior server's job, and the mushroom is rarer on menus than the Level III Black Trumpet, so it sits at Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is a yellowfoot just a small chanterelle?
proposals.menuLine: Roasted duck breast, yellowfoot chanterelles, celery root, huckleberry jus

proposals.reason: A small wild California milk-cap (Lactarius rubidus and its relatives). Dried, it smells powerfully of maple syrup, from sotolon, the same compound found in fenugreek. Pastry chefs at refined West Coast restaurants print it on ice creams, custards and panna cotta. It is the one mushroom a guest meets on the dessert menu, and the rarest, most specialist product in this list: a true Chef word. No card or alias covers it.
proposals.guestsAsk: There's a mushroom in the dessert? What does it taste like?
proposals.menuLine: Candy cap panna cotta, roasted pear, brown butter crumble

dispositions.reason: Dropped by the reconciler to hold the section at five, and no challenger raised it. It is printed mainly in the Pacific Northwest, so it is regional rather than a word a fine-dining server meets nationally. It is also best explained against the Perigord black truffle, which the deck does not yet teach. Revisit it once Black Truffle has a card; it could then be a seeAlso or a note there.

Not added in this run, which builds Level IV only. The challenger itself places it at Level III and the Lexicon candidate black-truffle is Level 3. It is the biggest hole in the section and should be FLAGGED FIRST for the next Level III run: term Black Truffle, aliases Perigord Truffle / Périgord Truffle / Winter Truffle / Tartufo Nero, lexiconSlug black-truffle. Today the Summer Truffle card's guest line refers to 'the winter one' with no card behind it.

The deck already teaches it. The Summer Truffle card (fd_0323) carries the note 'The same species dug in autumn is sold as Burgundy truffle, darker inside and more fragrant.' A separate card would duplicate a word the deck teaches. The right fix is to add 'Burgundy Truffle' as an alias on fd_0323 so search finds it. That is an edit to an existing card, not a new card at Level IV.

Added at Level IV. It is printed on winter menus, no card or alias covers it, and it belongs to this section's 'names one mushroom hides behind' role: it sits between the Chanterelle and Black Trumpet cards. 'Winter Chanterelle' is folded into its reason as the second menu name.

A real menu word with no card, but it does not make the five for this Level IV run. It is a cultivated mushroom now common on farm-to-table and Italian menus, so by the standard it reads as a Level III specialist product, beside the Level III Hedgehog Mushroom, more than as a rare Chef word. The five chosen are rarer or carry a harder question. Flag it for the next Level III run (aliases Pioppini, Black Poplar Mushroom).

Real in Japanese cooking and on some kaiseki menus, but rarely printed at the American fine-dining restaurants the deck serves. When it appears, it is usually inside a miso soup that the server explains as the dish, not by its mushroom. It is weaker on the 'on real menus or asked about' test than the five chosen.

Amanita caesarea is a classical Italian dish (insalata di ovoli), but fresh ovoli are almost never imported or printed on American menus, partly because of the amanita safety concern. It is a textbook-and-Italy word rather than a word an American fine-dining server meets, so it fails the 'not a word from a textbook only' test for this deck.

Out of this section and out of this run. It is a classical preparation (finely chopped mushrooms and shallot cooked down), not a mushroom or a truffle, and the challenger rates it Level III. Flag it for the Level III run of whichever section owns classical preparations (methods or sauces); it is printed constantly with Beef Wellington and has no card anywhere in the deck.

missing: Black Truffle [3]: no card anywhere in the deck. The section teaches White Truffle and Summer Truffle (and lists Black Summer Truffle as an alias) but not the winter Perigord truffle itself, which is the black truffle most fine-dining menus actually print ('shaved black winter truffle', 'Perigord truffle'). Lexicon slug: black-truffle. Its level is III, so it is outside this run, but it is the biggest hole in the section, and the Bianchetto and Oregon cards are explained by comparison with it. Alias: Perigord Truffle (menus print 'Périgord').

Burgundy Truffle [4]: printed on autumn menus from September to December as the step between summer and Perigord. Guests ask why it costs more than a summer truffle and less than a Perigord. The card has to say it is the same species as the Summer Truffle card (Tuber aestivum, sold as uncinatum) harvested ripe in autumn, with darker flesh and a hazelnut aroma, so a writer does not let it collapse into an alias.

Yellowfoot Chanterelle [4]: printed on winter menus ('yellowfoot chanterelles'). It is neither the golden Chanterelle nor the Black Trumpet, though it is in the trumpet's genus. No card has it as an alias. Menus also print it as 'Winter Chanterelle'.

Pioppino [4]: menus print it as 'pioppini' or 'pioppino mushrooms' (black poplar mushroom, Agrocybe). It is a regular on farm-to-table and Italian menus, and guests ask what it is. No card or alias covers it.
Nameko [4]: the small amber, gelatinous-capped mushroom found in miso soups and on kaiseki or omakase tasting menus. Guests ask about the slippery texture. No card covers it.

Ovoli [4]: Caesar's mushroom (Amanita caesarea), shaved raw in an 'insalata di ovoli' with Parmigiano at classical Italian fine-dining restaurants in autumn. Guests who know food ask whether an amanita is safe to eat.

Duxelles [3]: the finely chopped mushroom-and-shallot reduction inside Beef Wellington and under many en croute dishes, printed on menus and asked about constantly. No card anywhere in the deck. It is Level III and a preparation, so it may belong in a methods or sauces section rather than here; flag it for whichever section owns classical preparations.
sections.note:
I propose five words, all at Level 4 as this run asks. I checked each against everyCard by term and alias.

One gap I left out on purpose. The Périgord (black winter) truffle, Tuber melanosporum, is the Lexicon candidate 'black-truffle' at Level 3. It is a real hole in the section: the deck has White Truffle and Summer Truffle, but not the most important black truffle. By the standard it sits at Level 3, alongside White Truffle, so it belongs in a Level 3 run and not here. If it is added, it needs a printed term that cannot clash with the existing alias 'Black Summer Truffle'.

Words I considered and dropped:
- **Burgundy Truffle:** Tuber uncinatum is now treated as the same species as Summer Truffle, so it is close to an alias.
- **Yellowfoot (winter) chanterelle:** a guest would hear it as a chanterelle variant.
- **Pioppino:** closer to Level 3.
- **Duxelles and Forestière:** these are preparations, not mushrooms, so they belong to Preparations or Sauces.
- **Cauliflower Mushroom:** too rare on menus.

proposals.reason: A specialist style word on serious cheese courses (Comté d'Alpage, Gruyère d'Alpage, Beaufort Chalet d'Alpage). It means the wheel was made in a high mountain hut from summer-pasture milk, so it tastes of flowers and grass and costs more. Explaining why one Gruyère differs from another is a cheese-cart captain's job, which puts it at Chef even though the Lexicon rates it III. It is rare on American menus and no card teaches it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does 'd'alpage' mean, and why does this Gruyère cost more than the other one?
proposals.menuLine: Gruyère d'Alpage, 18 months, honeycomb, walnut bread

proposals.reason: The washed-rind cheese a food-literate guest names first, and the one on a fine-dining cheese cart that most needs a warning: it is very pungent, the paste runs, and the rind is washed in marc de Bourgogne. The deck teaches Washed Rind as a style at IV but no named washed-rind cheese. Taleggio and Robiola already have cards as named cheeses, so it fits this section, and it is rarer and more classical than either.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is it true Époisses was banned on the Paris Métro? How strong is it, and can I eat the rind?
proposals.menuLine: Époisses de Bourgogne, marc-washed, poached pear, spiced bread

proposals.reason: A style word on cheese courses for goat's-milk cheeses dusted with vegetable ash (Valençay, Selles-sur-Cher, cendré in French). The ash lowers the acidity at the surface so the rind can ripen, and that leaves the grey line or coat guests point at. The guest's question about whether the ash is safe has a simple answer; the why takes specialist knowledge. No card teaches it, and Chèvre (II) covers only the fresh cheese. It completes the rind-style words with Bloomy Rind (III) and Washed Rind (IV).
proposals.guestsAsk: What is the black layer? Is that ash, and can I eat it?
proposals.menuLine: Ash-ripened goat's milk pyramid, lavender honey, pistachio

dispositions.reason: Dropped from this run. Cabot Clothbound and similar wheels are on ordinary good American cheese boards, and one sentence explains them (cheddar wrapped in larded muslin and cave-aged, so it is drier and earthier). That is a Sous Chef specialist product next to Bloomy Rind (III), and this run builds only Level IV. Keep it for a Level III pass.

A real and important floor word, because the pregnancy and safety question matters. But by the standard it is not rare or deeply specialist: 'raw milk' and 'lait cru' are printed on many cheese menus, and guests ask about them often, which places it at Sous Chef (III). This run builds Level IV only, and the slot went to the rarer Mont d'Or. Keep it for a Level III pass, where it should be high priority.

Added at IV. It is a seasonal luxury showpiece (baked whole in its spruce box) and exactly the 'luxury and seasonal product' the Chef level lacks. It is named Mont d'Or so it cannot collide with custards fd_0348 Vacherin (Vacherin Glacé). It replaces the dropped Clothbound.

A genuine cart showpiece, but it is rarely printed on American fine-dining menus next to the other candidates, and the section is capped at five. Époisses and Mont d'Or carry the named-cheese slots with more menu presence.

Bordier is a proprietary brand (Jean-Yves Bordier), and a staff deck should teach the category, not a producer. The category, cultured or churned butter (beurre de baratte), is a common good-restaurant word that needs a sentence, which makes it Level II to III, outside this run. Beurre Monté holds the senior butter slot.

It does appear on Nordic-leaning tasting menus, but a guest's question takes one sentence ('the liquid left after the curds form'), and the Ricotta card already explains it in its body. It lacks the rarity or classical depth of the five chosen words, and the section is capped at five.

A legitimate cheese-course word, but it appears as a producer credit line, not as a dish or style word on the menu. It also ranks below the five chosen words for how often guests ask about it. Revisit it if the section's cap rises or a later pass adds cheese-course service words.

challenges.because: Cabot Clothbound and Montgomery's sit on nearly every good American cheese board and wine-bar plate, not only fine-dining carts, and one sentence covers it (cheddar wrapped in larded muslin and cave-aged, so it is drier and earthier than block). That is a Sous Chef specialist product next to Bloomy Rind (III), not a Chef word. It does not belong in this Level 4 run.

missing: Raw Milk [4]: printed as 'raw cow's milk' or 'lait cru' on serious cheese courses; guests ask whether it is legal or aged long enough and whether it is safe in pregnancy, and the answer (60-day rule, which cheeses carry it) takes a senior server; no card or alias teaches it

Mont d'Or [4]: seasonal (Oct-Mar) spruce-banded washed-rind cheese, often baked whole and spooned; menus print 'Vacherin Mont d'Or' or 'Mont d'Or', so name the card Mont d'Or, because the custards card fd Vacherin (Vacherin Glacé) is the meringue dessert and the two must not collide
Tête de Moine [4]: the cheese shaved into rosettes on a girolle at the cart, a fine-dining showpiece guests ask about ('why is it curled like that?'); untaught

Bordier Butter [4]: the named Breton beurre de baratte (churned, cultured, often seaweed or yuzu) printed on bread service at tasting-menu restaurants; guests ask why the butter is named; no butter card covers a named or cultured butter

Whey [4]: printed on Nordic-leaning and tasting menus (whey-glazed, whey caramel, fermented whey, whey beurre blanc); guests ask what it is; it appears only inside the Ricotta card body, never as a term
Affineur [4]: cheese courses credit the ager ('aged by Jasper Hill Cellars', 'Hervé Mons, affineur'); a guest who knows cheese asks what the affineur did to it; untaught
sections.note: I propose five words, all at Level 4, the top of the allowed range. Two other Level 4 words came close and were cut to stay within five. Tomme is the mountain-style name on cheese courses (Tomme de Savoie, Tomme Crayeuse). Raw Milk / Lait Cru is a word guests ask about, especially about pregnancy and the US rule that raw-milk cheese must age 60 days. Either could replace Ash-Ripened or Clothbound if the reconciler wants a different mix. I chose not to propose Mont d'Or, because Vacherin is already a Level 4 dessert card (custards) and the name would invite confusion. Cultured Butter and Clotted Cream are real menu words but sit at Level 2 or 3, so this run leaves them out. Alpage carries the Lexicon slug alpage-cheeses-summer-milk, which the Lexicon rates at Level III; I place it at IV for the floor reason given in its entry.

proposals.reason: Piedmont's egg pasta, made from a dough that is almost all yolk (menus print '40 yolks') and cut much finer than tagliatelle. It is the white-truffle-season signature at serious Italian and tasting-menu kitchens. The deck teaches Tagliatelle (II) and White Truffle (III, mushrooms) but has no card for this pasta under any name. A captain has to explain the yolk dough, the fine cut and why it carries shaved truffle or butter and sage. That is regional and specialist, so it is Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is tajarin, and how is it different from tagliatelle?
proposals.menuLine: Tajarin, 40-yolk dough, brown butter, shaved Alba white truffle (supplement)

proposals.reason: A single large raviolo around ricotta and a whole raw yolk that stays runny when the raviolo is cut. It is the San Domenico (Imola) classic, still served on tasting menus and often printed as 'egg yolk raviolo'. The Ravioli card (I) teaches the square pillow, not this dish. The server has to explain how the yolk stays liquid (it cooks for only a few minutes) and how to eat it. A deeply classical dish that knowing guests test on belongs at Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: How does the yolk stay runny inside the raviolo?
proposals.menuLine: Uovo in raviolo, ricotta, farm egg yolk, brown butter, Parmigiano Reggiano

proposals.reason: Ligurian coin-shaped pasta pressed with a carved wooden stamp. It appears on chef-driven Italian menus with pesto, walnut sauce or marjoram, and guests always ask because the name tells them nothing. The deck has no stamped pasta. Explaining it takes the stamp, the region and why the embossed face holds a light sauce. That is specialist pasta-shape vocabulary, so it is Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: What are corzetti, and what's the pattern pressed into them?
proposals.menuLine: Hand-stamped corzetti, Ligurian walnut sauce, marjoram, Taggiasca olives

proposals.reason: The Veneto's IGP semifino risotto rice, the grain of a loose Venetian risotto all'onda. Fine-dining menus name it the way they name Carnaroli (III) and Acquerello (IV). It completes the risotto-rice set a sommelier-minded captain is tested on, and no card or alias teaches it. It is rarer on menus than Carnaroli and needs real explaining (a smaller grain that drinks broth fast and finishes in a loose wave), so it sits at Chef next to Acquerello.
proposals.guestsAsk: Why Vialone Nano instead of Arborio or Carnaroli?
proposals.menuLine: Risotto all'onda, Vialone Nano, spring peas, Parmigiano Reggiano 36 months

proposals.reason: Rice grits: the broken pieces of Carolina Gold rice left after milling. Anson Mills revived them, and refined Southern and Lowcountry menus now print them, cooked like risotto or grits. The deck teaches Grits (I) and Carolina Gold (III) but not this product. Guests take it for a typo or a corn product, so the server has to explain that it is broken heirloom rice that cooks creamy like risotto. It is the one American heirloom-grain word in this list, and a heritage specialist product belongs at Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: What are middlins? Is that grits?
proposals.menuLine: Carolina Gold rice middlins, Lowcountry shrimp, country ham broth, benne

dispositions.reason: Dropped from the proposals to keep five. It would have been the fifth Italian specialty out of five, and Middlins gives American heirloom grain its one place. It is a real menu word and guests do ask why the pasta is dark, so it is the first reserve for a later run.
Added at Level 4. It is a classical tasting-menu dish that guests ask about by name, and the Ravioli card (I) does not teach it. It took the slot Grano Arso left.

A real word, but it loses the slot. The section already teaches three stuffed pastas (Agnolotti, Ravioli, Tortellini), and Corzetti and Uovo in Raviolo already cover the regional pasta and the tasting-menu pasta. Culurgiones appear on American menus less often than either. Second reserve for a later run.

A pasta of Valtellina trattorias and Alpine home cooking that rarely appears on American fine-dining menus. If the grey buckwheat pasta matters, the Buckwheat card (II) can mention it in a line, without a Chef card of its own.

Menus print it as provenance on a house pasta ('Senatore Cappelli durum'), and guests rarely stop to ask about it. A server can read it out as 'a heritage durum wheat' without owning a card. If the heritage-wheat slot is ever filled, Grano Arso is the stronger word for it.

Calasparra is a Murcian D.O., not a separate kind of rice. The D.O. grows Bomba itself, sold as 'Calasparra Bomba'. 'Bomba or Calasparra?' is therefore a question about where the rice was grown, and the Bomba card (III) can answer it in a line. American menus print Bomba far more often.

It is the crust a paella pan makes, the result of cooking rather than a grain, rice or pasta, so it fits this section's 'what each one is' only loosely. It also appears mainly on Spanish specialists' menus. The Bomba card (III) is the natural place to teach it: the rice that stays separate is the rice that crusts.

An Anson Mills heirloom corn printed by only a handful of kitchens as 'Otto File polenta'. Guests read it as provenance and rarely ask about it. Middlins already fills the one heritage-mill slot with the word guests stumble on more often.

missing: Culurgiones [4]: Sardinian potato, pecorino and mint dumplings with a pleated wheat-ear seal. Chef-driven Italian menus print them and every guest asks, and no card covers them (Fregola is the deck's only Sardinian starch).

Uovo in Raviolo [4]: one large raviolo around a runny yolk, the San Domenico classic that tasting menus still serve. Guests ask how the yolk stays liquid. The Ravioli card (Level I) does not teach it.

Pizzoccheri [4]: short buckwheat tagliatelle from the Valtellina, served with cabbage, potato and Bitto or Casera. The Buckwheat card teaches the seed, not this pasta, and guests ask why the pasta is grey.

Senatore Cappelli [4]: the heritage durum wheat that refined Italian menus name for their house pasta, the way they name Carnaroli or Acquerello for rice. It sits next to Grano Arso and the deck has no card for it.
Calasparra [4]: the D.O. rice from Murcia printed on paella menus beside Bomba. Without it a captain cannot answer 'Bomba or Calasparra?' The Bomba card (Level III) does not alias it.
Socarrat [4]: the toasted crust of rice on the bottom of a paella pan, which serious paella menus promise and knowing guests ask for by name. Bomba teaches the rice but not the crust.

Otto File [4]: Eight Row Flint, the heirloom Italian-American flint corn that refined menus name for their polenta ("Otto File polenta"). The Polenta card (II) teaches the dish but not the heritage corn.
sections.note: All five are Level IV. I matched every term and plausible alias against the 336 cards in everyCard and none of the five is already taught. The brief's Lexicon candidates hold no starch term, so no slug is given. Words I left out: Agnolotti del Plin, because it is a variant of the existing Agnolotti card. Pici and Bigoli, because they read as Level III. Koshihikari, Culurgiones, Cappellacci and Casoncelli are fair alternates if any of the five is rejected; they are rarer on American menus or closer to Level III. Grano Arso is the least common of the five on menus, so it is the first to swap out (for Koshihikari or Culurgiones). The brief's "aims" say two to four per section while the run asks for three to five; I followed the run's three to five.

proposals.reason: This is the emulsified butter bath behind the butter-poached lobster of American fine dining, and menus in the Keller line print it by name. A senior server has to separate it from Beurre Blanc (taught at III). Monté is butter held emulsified in a little water, with no wine, vinegar or shallot reduction. It works as a cooking bath and a glaze, not as an acid sauce. The difference takes real explaining and guests who know food test it, so it is Level IV. No card or alias covers it: Clarified, Brown and Compound Butter are different preparations.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is beurre monté, and is it just melted butter?
proposals.menuLine: Maine lobster poached in beurre monté, sweet corn, chanterelles, tarragon

proposals.reason: This is hollandaise finished with blood-orange juice and zest. In spring, French and fine-dining menus print it beside white and green asparagus. The guest's question is always what separates it from hollandaise, which the deck teaches at I. A server needs the parent sauce, the blood orange and the season to answer that, which makes it a specialist classical word. It sits at Level IV and is taught under no term or alias.
proposals.guestsAsk: What's the difference between sauce maltaise and hollandaise?
proposals.menuLine: White asparagus, sauce maltaise, blood orange, chervil

proposals.reason: This is the classical lobster sauce: shells roasted with tomato, shallot, cognac and white wine, reduced, then mounted with butter. French-leaning fine-dining menus put it under lobster, sole and monkfish. The name misleads, because guests ask whether it is American, so the server must explain what goes into the pot and the américaine/armoricaine naming dispute. It is rare, classical and specialist, so it is Level IV. No lobster sauce or bisque is taught under another name.
proposals.guestsAsk: Sauce américaine, so is it an American sauce? What's it made from?
proposals.menuLine: Pan-roasted monkfish, sauce américaine, fennel confit, saffron potatoes

proposals.reason: This is the classical black-truffle sauce: demi-glace reduced with Madeira and finished with chopped black truffle, named for Périgord. In winter truffle season, French and luxury tasting menus print it beside tournedos Rossini, foie gras and squab. Explaining it takes the truffle, the Madeira and the demi-glace, and guests who know the classics ask about it, so it is Level IV. The deck teaches Truffle and Demi-Glace but not this sauce.
proposals.guestsAsk: What's in sauce Périgueux? Is it made with real truffle?
proposals.menuLine: Beef tenderloin Rossini, seared foie gras, brioche, sauce Périgueux

proposals.reason: This is the Jura cream sauce built on vin jaune, an oxidative, sherry-like wine aged under a veil of yeast. Its classic partners are chicken and morels (poulet au vin jaune). Refined French menus and wine-led American menus print it as 'sauce vin jaune', 'vin jaune sauce' or 'vin jaune cream'. The card teaches the sauce, and through it the wine, which is the part a sommelier-minded captain is tested on. Both need explaining, so it is Level IV. The deck teaches Morel and Velouté but no Jura wine sauce.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is vin jaune? Is that a wine, and could I order a glass of it with this?
proposals.menuLine: Roast poularde, morels, sauce vin jaune, pommes purée

dispositions.reason: Dropped. The challenger is right that in America it is mostly a book word, seen only at an occasional Escoffier tribute dinner. The menu line was also wrong: poularde demi-deuil is classically served with sauce suprême. Its parent Suprême means the cut on today's menus, which belongs in meats. The slot goes to Sauce Maltaise, a word that actually appears on menus.

The proposal stands as the sauce. A card named only 'Vin Jaune' names a wine, and the brief requires every card to belong to this section, whose blurb covers sauces. A bare wine card would belong with drinks, not with sauces, stocks and dressings. The challenger's real point is accepted inside the card: the reason, guest question and menu line teach the wine through the sauce. The reason also lists the common printings ('vin jaune sauce', 'vin jaune cream'), so a server recognises each form.

Added at Level IV. White and spring asparagus menus print it every spring, and guests ask how it differs from hollandaise (taught at I). It is taught under no term or alias. It replaces Albufera because it shows up on real menus far more often.

It is real and classical, but in the US it is now limited to a few old-guard French rooms serving pike quenelles. It shows up on menus less than the five kept here. The Quenelle card in preparations is the natural place to name it as the classic partner. It is first in line if the section ever goes past five.

It names a way of preparing a game bird (the bird cooked, then its carcass pressed and reduced into its own sauce) more than a freestanding sauce, so it belongs to preparations or meats rather than this section. It is also rarer on US menus than the five kept.

Only the handful of US rooms that run a duck press print it, and they usually print the dish ('pressed duck', 'canard à la presse') rather than the sauce's name. The word guests ask about is the press, which belongs with duck in meats or preparations. In this section it would be a book word.

It is a fair Level IV word on autumn venison menus. It loses on the five-word limit to Périgueux, which luxury menus print more often. Bordelaise (III) already gives a server the brown wine reduction under red meat. It is first in line with Nantua if the section takes more.

On US menus 'pil pil' most often means shrimp sizzled in chili-garlic oil (gambas al pil pil), which is not the Basque gelatin emulsion the challenger describes. A card would teach a meaning that clashes with most of the menus a server actually sees. Where it is printed, it names a Spanish dish preparation rather than a sauce in this section's classical sense, and the five-word limit is already full.

challenges.because: A book word in America. In twenty years I have not seen it on a US menu outside a chef's Escoffier tribute dinner, and no guest has asked about it. The 'isn't that the paella lagoon' question is invented. Poularde demi-deuil is classically served with sauce suprême, not Albufera, so the menu line also fails. If the section needs a poultry cream sauce, it has to wait until Suprême is on menus as a sauce. On menus today Suprême means the cut, and that belongs in meats.

Menus do not print a fixed 'Sauce Vin Jaune'. They print 'vin jaune sauce', 'vin jaune cream', 'morels in vin jaune' and 'sauce au vin jaune', and the word guests test you on is the wine itself. Name the card by the word that is constant, Vin Jaune, and teach the sauce in it. Then it also covers the Comté pairing and the wine-list line.

missing: Sauce Maltaise [4]: blood-orange hollandaise. It is printed with white asparagus and spring asparagus on French and fine-dining menus, and guests ask what makes it different from hollandaise (Hollandaise is taught at I, Maltaise under no term or alias).

Sauce Nantua [4]: crayfish butter and cream sauce, the classical partner of quenelles de brochet ('pike quenelles, sauce Nantua'). It is on classical French menus in the US and guests ask what Nantua is. Quenelle is taught in preparations, but the sauce is not.

Salmis [4]: game bird (squab, duck, pheasant) whose carcass is pressed and reduced with red wine into the sauce for its own meat. Tasting menus print 'squab salmis' and 'salmis sauce'. It is deeply classical and needs explaining.

Sauce Rouennaise [4]: the blood-thickened sauce of pressed duck (canard à la presse; menus also say 'sauce au sang'). Where a duck press runs it is the showpiece, and every table asks how it works. Moulard and Duck Breast are taught, but this sauce is not.

Sauce Poivrade [4]: peppery brown game sauce (Grand Veneur is its venison child, with red-currant jelly and cream) printed beside venison and hare in autumn. Guests ask whether it is just pepper sauce. Venison is taught, but no game sauce is.

Pil Pil [4]: the Basque emulsion of olive oil and the gelatin from salt cod skin, made by swirling the cazuela ('bacalao al pil pil', 'hake pil pil'). It is on Spanish and Basque menus in the US and is asked about by name. Emulsion and Aioli do not cover it.
sections.note: I propose five words, all at Level IV, as this run asked; Level III was not wanted. None of the five matches a Lexicon candidate in the brief, so none has a slug. I checked each against everyCard: no card holds it as a term or an alias, and none is a spelling variant of a card. Words I considered and left out: Dashi, Bagna Cauda, Rouille, Sauce Vierge, XO Sauce and Fumet are better at Level III or belong to another run. Beurre Rouge is too close to the Beurre Blanc card. Choron, Foyot and Maltaise are Béarnaise and Hollandaise variants that turn up more in books than on today's American menus. Five is the honest limit for Level IV in this section.

proposals.reason: Deeply classical and still printed on charcuterie and first-course menus at French fine-dining rooms: a bird or fish boned whole, stuffed, rolled, poached and served cold, often glazed in its own gelée. It pairs with Ballotine, which the deck teaches at IV, and that pair is exactly the confusable a knowing guest tests. No card or alias in everyCard holds it (Terrine, Pâté, Torchon, Roulade and Ballotine all differ), and it belongs to this section's stuffed-and-rolled words. No Lexicon candidate holds it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What's the difference between a galantine and a ballotine?
proposals.menuLine: Duck Galantine, pistachio, cherry mostarda, pickled shallot, toasted brioche

proposals.reason: A domed pie of two puff-pastry rounds sealed over a filling, scored in curved rays: game, duck or foie gras at fine-dining tables, often a dish for two cut tableside. It is a printed word at refined American restaurants and cannot be decoded from the menu. The deck teaches En Croûte and Puff Pastry but not this named form, and it fits the section's baked-under-a-crust words.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is a pithivier, and is it like a pot pie?
proposals.menuLine: Pheasant & Foie Gras Pithivier for two, black truffle, sauce périgueux

proposals.reason: French for 'half-cooked'. Fine-dining menus print it on foie gras, salmon, tuna and chocolate courses, and guests reliably ask whether the dish is raw. It sits with Torchon and Crudo among this section's raw-and-cured instruction words, and no card or alias in everyCard holds it. Added from the challenger's missing list. No Lexicon candidate holds it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does mi-cuit mean, is it raw?
proposals.menuLine: Foie Gras Mi-Cuit, Sauternes gelée, quince, toasted brioche

proposals.reason: The classic French garnish named for the composer: beef tenderloin on a crouton topped with seared foie gras and black truffle, with Madeira or Périgueux sauce. Fine-dining and luxury steakhouse menus print it, usually as a costly supplement, so guests test the server on it. It belongs with the section's named classic finishes (Meunière, Grenobloise, Amandine), and the deck holds it under no term or alias.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does Rossini mean on the filet?
proposals.menuLine: Tournedos Rossini, seared foie gras, black truffle, Madeira jus, pommes purée

dispositions.reason: Dropped to keep the section at five. The rolled-and-stuffed family already has Roulade (II) and Ballotine (IV), and Galantine now joins them. On American menus Paupiette mostly shows up as one famous signature dish (Daniel's sea bass), so the raw/cured and named-finish words it would displace (Mi-Cuit, Kombujime, Rossini) are printed far more often. It is a sound word to hold for a later run.
Added at IV. Fine-dining menus print it widely on foie gras, fish and chocolate, guests ask whether it is raw, no card or alias holds it, and it fits the section's raw-and-cured instruction words.
